Hi, I'm Kelsey! I am a mixed-methods researcher working at the intersection of sociology and computational social science.
My research started with an ethnographic question: how do communities construct their own norms, and what happens when you look closely at who gets to belong and who doesn't? For my senior thesis, I designed and led a multi-year ethnographic study examining power and norm enforcement within party subcultures. I did a cultural comparison of two college party subcultures in the same neighborhood (frat parties and house shows), with 30+ interviews and 30+ hours of participant observation. I developed the concept of "privilege bargaining" to explain how individuals manage their privilege-  a political strategy in seemingly "apolitical" spaces.  

From there, I spent several years doing applied qualitative and mixed-methods research in social policy, studying workforce training, housing, and economic mobility at MDRC, before moving into UX and platform research, where I study how people interact with digital technologies and AI-mediated environments. These may seem disparate, but my connecting focus is how communities, online and off, construct norms, and how both platforms and spaces mediate that. 

I'm currently finishing an MS in Applied Quantitative Research for Social Analysis at Northeastern, concentrating in Computational Social Science, and building a toolkit that spans statistical modeling, machine learning and computational text analysis. I work primarily in R, with growing proficiency in Python and SQL.

I recently completed an intensive in Distant Reading, NLP, and sentiment analysis (all in R) at the European Summer University in Digital Humanities, and I'm now turning those tools on the questions I've always cared about most for a thesis about online communities. More on that soon!
